sources.citation: Sutton, Peter. 2001. Talking language in party mode: some cases from Cape York Peninsula. In Simpson et al. (eds), Forty years on: Ken Hale and Australian languages, 453-464. Pacific Linguistics 512.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: p.457 lists Wik-Keyenganh among like-named variety names ('language + move'); fn.16: 'I hyphenate proper names of linguistic varieties such as Wik-Mungkan or Wik-Ngathan because they are single phonological words with primary stress on the first syllable.' This is about the variety names as words, not a description of Wik-Keyenganh word stress.

sources.citation: Sutton, Peter John. 1978. Wik: Aboriginal society, territory and language at Cape Keerweer, Cape York Peninsula, Australia. PhD thesis, University of Queensland (ANU Open Research hdl:1885/307607)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing about Wik-Keyangan. p.40: Sutton's own data include only 'fragments of Wik-Ayangenycha and Wik-Keyangan'; p.109: 'Wik-Keyangan probably belongs with the dialects of language 4 [Kugu-Muminh, Kugu-Uwanh], but I have insufficient data to assign it with confidence'; ch. IV: 3 speakers, 'only one, two or three knowledgeable speakers left (Me, Ke)'; p.218: one comparative lexical item (34 'Children') recorded for Ke. The Appendix 1 stress statement (p.235, primary stress on the first vowel of the word) is explicitly scoped to Wik-Ngathana, not Wik-Keyangan.

sources.citation: Sutton, Peter & Ken Hale. 2021. Linguistic Organisation and Native Title: The Wik Case, Australia. Canberra: ANU Press (Asia-Pacific Linguistics). doi:10.22459/LONT.2021
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing for Wik-Keyenganh. It appears only as a dialect name: p.58 (Dixon 2002 Bc2 Wik-Me'nh, other dialects Wik-Ep (= Wik-Iit), Wik-Keyenganh); pp.81-84, 90 (one estate, 15-25 people); p.129 dialect set 4 (a) Wik-Ep = Wik-Iit; (b) Wik-Me'enh; (c) Wik-Keyenganh; clan entries. The book's stress remarks (pp.60 fn.31, 181-182) concern Wik-Way, Wik-Ngathan/Ngatharr, Wik-Mungkan.
